documents.title: Honor Code (includes Generative AI rule)
documents.stance_why: The Honor Code says AI 'should not be used in the completion of any course assignments, exams, or written work... unless an instructor... has specifically and explicitly authorized their use'. AI is banned unless permitted, so restrict rather than delegates, because a default ban is set.
documents.summary: The undergraduate Honor Code is a long student-governance document covering the Honor Board, hearing procedures, appeals and academic and social resolutions. A single paragraph in the academic resolutions sets the AI rule: no generative AI on coursework unless an instructor explicitly authorizes it, and undisclosed, unattributed or exam use is an Honor Code violation. The rest of the document supplies the general integrity and enforcement process that applies to such violations.

units.why: The sentence says generative AI tools "should not be used in the completion of any course assignments, exams, or written work", so the default for all coursework is a ban. P01 (default prohibition) rather than P06 because it sets the rule for all coursework, not the fallback for a silent syllabus; the instructor exception is coded separately as P04.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P01, actor, phase and modality; they differed only on anchor span and policy wording (A put the instructor exception into the policy, B used a null policy with a shorter anchor). The source sentence holds the ban and the exception; the exception is its own unit (P04), so the policy states the ban only, in the source's wording.
units.anchor: Generative AI tools should not be used in the completion of any course assignments
units.policy: Generative AI tools should not be used in the completion of any course assignments, exams, or written work, including laboratory work.

units.why: The exception "unless an instructor for a given course has specifically and explicitly authorized their use for the assignment in question" makes permission an instructor, per-assignment decision. P04 (who decides) rather than P06, since it names the decision-maker, not the silent-syllabus fallback.
units.resolution_why: Coder A: actor instructor, phase before-course. Coder B: actor all, phase during-work. Both chose P04, may, restrict. The source makes the instructor the one who authorizes AI 'for the assignment in question', so the rule is about the instructor's authorization decision; I keep actor instructor and before-course (authorization is set when the assignment is designed). I use A's normalized policy because the anchor alone omits the 'only' framing, and it adds nothing beyond the source.
units.anchor: unless an instructor for a given course has specifically and explicitly authorized their use
units.policy: Generative AI use is allowed only where the instructor for a given course has specifically and explicitly authorized it for the assignment in question.

units.why: "Presenting AI-generated content as original student work" is named as a violation of the Honor Code, which bars having AI produce what a student submits as their own. P19 rather than P36 because the content of the prohibited act is the point; the label 'violation' is carried in the wording.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on every code; they differed on policy (A null, B normalized) and on one topic (A accountability-understanding, B integrity-sanctions). The source calls the act a violation of the Honor Code, so a normalized policy that includes this is more faithful than a bare anchor, and integrity-sanctions fits the violation label.
units.anchor: Presenting AI-generated content as original student work
units.policy: Presenting AI-generated content as original student work is a violation of the Honor Code.

units.why: "submitting AI-generated content without citing its source in artificial intelligence tools" is called a violation, so students must cite or disclose AI-generated content. P24 (disclose with each submission), not P28, since nothing is said about how disclosure affects grading.
units.resolution_why: Coder A: unit_stance permit. Coder B: require. Both chose P24, must. The codebook reserves 'require' for AI use built into or required by the work. The passage makes uncited AI content a violation, so cited and authorized AI content is tolerable: a condition on use, hence permit.
units.anchor: submitting AI-generated content without citing its source
units.policy: Submitting AI-generated content without citing its source in artificial intelligence tools is a violation of the Honor Code.

units.why: "relying on generative AI tools for closed-book quizzes, tests, and exams" is called a violation, so AI is barred in closed-book assessments. P22 is the exact type for no AI on exams and quizzes.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on all codes; they differed on policy (A null, B normalized). The anchor does not say 'violation', so the normalized policy is used, matching the source sentence.
units.anchor: relying on generative AI tools for closed-book quizzes, tests, and exams
units.policy: Relying on generative AI tools for closed-book quizzes, tests, and exams is a violation of the Honor Code.

documents.title: Generative AI: Privacy and security guidelines (Ask Athena)
documents.stance_why: The page tells users to "Use College-provided AI tools" and to be careful with other tools, but sets no ban on AI and no per-course rule. It treats AI use as allowed with data, privacy and critical-evaluation conditions, so permit rather than delegates, and it defers academic limits to the Honor Code.
documents.summary: An IT help article on responsible use of generative AI with college data and systems. It points users to four college-provided tools, explains privacy and terms-of-service concerns, and warns about hallucination, bias, copyright, environmental cost and industry-sponsored claims. It tells students to follow the Honor Code and says nothing about course-level AI rules.

units.why: The page says the guidelines "support the responsible and ethical use of AI technology, while managing risk", stating the purpose of the framework. P56 (institution-wide framework) fits.
units.resolution_why: Coder A: unit_stance permit; B: neutral. Codes otherwise agree. The sentence is a purpose statement and does not itself permit or limit any use, so neutral. Topics merged to privacy-data and default-stance.
units.anchor: guidelines that support the responsible and ethical use of AI technology

units.why: "Use College-provided AI tools (Firefly, BoodleBox, Microsoft Copilot, Zoom AI Companion)" directs users to vetted tools, with the privacy note that follows as the reason. P50 (prefer vetted tools) rather than P17, because the point is data protection, not provision of a course tool.
units.resolution_why: Coder A: phase during-work; B: general. Type, modality and stance agree. The directive is about which tool to pick when doing work, so during-work.
units.anchor: Use College-provided AI tools (Firefly, BoodleBox, Microsoft Copilot, Zoom AI Companion)

units.why: The note says the tools' terms ensure inputs and outputs "will not be used to train AI models or answer AI queries made by others", the factual basis for preferring College tools. P50 (data protection), informs.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on all codes; differed on policy (B normalized, A null). The anchor already states the content, so policy is null.
units.anchor: will not be used to train AI models or answer AI queries made by others

units.why: "Other tools -- especially free ones -- may lack these protections" warns that non-College tools give weaker data protection. A privacy fact, so P50, informs.
units.resolution_why: Only Coder A coded this as its own unit (Coder B folded it with the next sentence under one anchor). The sentence is a real statement, distinct from the instruction to review terms (fact versus directive), so I keep it as a separate unit.
units.anchor: Other tools -- especially free ones -- may lack these protections

units.why: "Always review a tool's terms of service and privacy policies carefully" tells users to check terms before use, a data-protection step. P50 rather than P52, which is about ownership and copyright of outputs.
units.resolution_why: Coder A: phase during-work; B: general. Codes otherwise agree. Reviewing terms precedes using a tool, so during-work.
units.anchor: Always review a tool's terms of service and privacy policies carefully

units.why: "if you must use free tools, avoid uploading private or sensitive information" limits what may be entered into non-vetted tools. P50 (protect personal data) is the match; P20 and P49 concern assignment materials.
units.resolution_why: Coder A: phase during-work; B: general. The instruction applies when entering data into a tool, so during-work.
units.anchor: if you must use free tools, avoid uploading private or sensitive information

units.why: "Follow all relevant College policies: Acceptable Use Policy, Data Handling Policy" binds AI use to existing institution-wide policies. P56 fits as a scope statement.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on all codes; differed on policy (A normalized, B null) and topics (B added default-stance). The anchor alone omits the two named policies, so the normalized policy is used; default-stance dropped since no stance is set.
units.anchor: Follow all relevant College policies
units.policy: Follow all relevant College policies, including the Acceptable Use Policy and the Data Handling Policy.

units.why: "Students must also adhere to their Honor Code" ties student AI use to the Honor Code. P56 (framework cross-reference) rather than P36 since no misconduct classification is stated here.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on all codes and differed only on anchor span. The full phrase states the rule, so policy is null.
units.anchor: Students must also adhere to their Honor Code

units.why: "Always critically evaluate any generative AI output." tells users to check AI output, the verify-output type. P31.
units.resolution_why: Coder A: phase during-work, modality should; B: general, must. Type agrees. The page is guidance, not a binding code, and its other 'always' directive is coded should; evaluating output happens while working, so should and during-work.
units.anchor: Always critically evaluate any generative AI output.

units.why: Tools "can predict things that are statistically plausible but inaccurate or without factual basis", including nonexistent citations. This explains why output must be verified, so P31, informs.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on all codes; differed on anchor span (A shorter). I use the fuller anchor so the inaccuracy claim is stated in full.
units.anchor: can predict things that are statistically plausible but inaccurate or without factual basis
units.frag_end: books and authors that do not exist!

units.why: The tools are "vulnerable to biases" in their training data. This names bias as a concern about AI, a point distinct from inaccuracy, so P53 (name bias, harms, environmental costs), informs.
units.resolution_why: Only Coder B coded bias separately (P53); Coder A folded it into the hallucination unit as a topic. The source sentence makes two claims (bias, inaccuracy) and bias fits P53, not P31, so I keep it as its own unit.
units.anchor: vulnerable to biases
units.frag_end: books and authors that do not exist!

units.why: "Look for settings that can help you critically evaluate a bot's output" recommends using tool modes that support checking, a way to act on the verification duty. P31.
units.resolution_why: Coder A: phase during-work, unit_stance neutral; B: general, encourage. The sentence recommends using certain features, so encourage; phase during-work as the features are used while working.
units.anchor: Look for settings that can help you critically evaluate a bot's output

units.why: "The applicability of copyright law, moral rights, and fair use to these tools is still under discussion" states legal uncertainty over AI use. P52 covers copyright and licensing.
units.anchor: applicability of copyright law,
units.policy: The applicability of copyright law, moral rights, and fair use to these tools is still under discussion.

units.why: Some products, such as Adobe Firefly, "prohibit users from uploading copyrighted materials without permission of the copyright holder", a tool-terms fact about copyright. P52 rather than P49 because the rule belongs to the tool, not the College.
units.anchor: prohibit users from uploading copyrighted materials without permission of the copyright holder

units.why: "AI processing is energy-intensive" and growth may offset efficiency gains: an environmental cost. P53.
units.anchor: AI processing is energy-intensive

units.why: Readers are told to "think critically about who authored and published this information and what they stand to gain" when reading claims about AI's promises or perils. This is source evaluation of AI discourse, not verification of AI output, so P31 does not fit and no other type does; UNCOVERED.
units.resolution_why: Coder A: UNCOVERED; Coder B: P31 (critical evaluation). P31 is defined as verifying AI output because it is often wrong; this passage is about the commercial interests behind stories about AI, not AI output. P53 does not fit either. I follow A.
units.anchor: be sure to think critically about who authored and published this information
units.uncovered_note: Advice to read claims about AI's promises and perils critically, since sources may be sponsored by AI vendors (information literacy about AI discourse).

units.why: "The College reserves the right to disconnect or disable, without warning or prior notice, any computer, account, or service that poses a security or performance threat" or violates College policies. It states a sanction the College may apply, so P37 (state penalties in advance), though it is an IT enforcement power and not AI-specific.
units.resolution_why: Only Coder A coded this (as UNCOVERED). It is a real statement on the AI guidelines page (under 'Appropriate use') and states a concrete consequence, disabling access without notice, for threats or policy violations. P37 fits as a concrete sanction stated in advance, so I keep it and assign P37 instead of UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: reserves the right to disconnect or disable, without warning or prior notice

units.why: The list of College-provided tools describes BoodleBox as "a collaborative AI workspace with access to many LLM models and privacy and teaching features", naming a sanctioned, licensed tool. P17.
units.resolution_why: Coder A: unit_stance encourage, normalized policy; B: neutral, null. The passage describes available tools and does not recommend them, so neutral; the anchor names the tool, and the policy is left null.
units.anchor: A collaborative AI workspace with access to many LLM models

notes: Reconciled A and B. Honor Code coded only for its generative-AI paragraph; Coder A's generic Honor Code procedure units (P29, P37, P54, P57, P64) and the P36 summary sentence were dropped as not about AI use or as repeats of the three violation units. LITS stance: A permit, B delegates; resolved to permit because the page allows AI use with data and evaluation conditions and does not hand the decision to instructors. The third collected document (bryn-mawr-lits-ai-page) was screened out and not coded. No school or computing policy found; course layer deferred.
